claim: Genetic ablation of SIRPα induced the emergence of CD11c+ microglia in the brain white matter.
source: To examine the role of SIRPα in microglial activation, brains of SIRPα knockout (KO) mice were subjected to immunohistochemical analysis using antibodies specific to Iba1, a microglia marker, and to CD68, a marker for phagocytically active microglia (Figure 1A). The numbers of Iba1+cells as well as of Iba1+/CD68+ cells in the white matter, such as the fimbria, were significantly increased in the brains of SIRPα KO mice compared with those of wild-type (WT) control mice, suggesting the activation of microglia in these regions (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data showing increased Iba1+ and Iba1+/CD68+ cells in SIRPα KO mice (Figure 1A and B), and by flow cytometry data showing increased CD11c+ microglia (Figure 1C and D, Figure 3B).

claim: The numbers of Iba1+ cells and Iba1+/CD68+ cells in the white matter were significantly increased in the brains of SIRPα KO mice compared with those of wild-type control mice.
source: The numbers of Iba1+cells as well as of Iba1+/CD68+ cells in the white matter, such as the fimbria, were significantly increased in the brains of SIRPα KO mice compared with those of wild-type (WT) control mice, suggesting the activation of microglia in these regions (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Quantitative analysis in Figure 1B shows statistically significant increases in both Iba1+ and Iba1+/CD68+ cell counts in SIRPα KO mice.

claim: The numbers of Iba1+ cells and EYFP+ cells were markedly increased in the white matter of SIRPα KO:CD11c–EYFP Tg mice when compared with that of control SIRPα WT:CD11c-EYFP Tg mice.
source: The numbers of Iba1+ cells and EYFP+ cells were markedly increased in the white matter (including the corpus callosum, external capsule, fimbria, and internal capsule) of SIRPα KO:CD11c–EYFP Tg mice when compared with that of control SIRPα WT:CD11c-EYFP Tg mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Figure 1C shows increased EYFP signal (CD11c reporter) in white matter regions of SIRPα KO mice.

claim: Most EYFP+ cells in the white matter of SIRPα KO mice were Iba1 positive, suggesting that they were CD11c+ microglia.
source: Most EYFP+ cells in the white matter of SIRPα KO mice were Iba1 positive, suggesting that they were CD11c+ microglia (Figure 1D lower panels).
evidence: Figure 1D shows colocalization of EYFP and Iba1 signals in white matter.

claim: The EYFP signal was barely detected in the grey matter of either genotype.
source: By contrast, the EYFP signal was barely detected in the grey matter of either genotype (Figure 1D upper panels).
evidence: Figure 1D upper panels show minimal EYFP signal in grey matter (ctx) of both genotypes.

claim: The white matter-specific emergence of Iba1+/CD11c+ cells was confirmed using an antibody specific to CD11c in the brain or spinal cord of SIRPα KO mice.
source: The white matter-specific emergence of Iba1+/CD11c+ cells was also confirmed using an antibody that is specific to CD11c in the brain or spinal cord of SIRPα KO mice (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Figure 2A and B show immunostaining with CD11c-specific antibody confirming increased CD11c+ cells in white matter regions.

claim: No appreciable demyelination was evident after immunostaining for myelin basic protein in SIRPα KO mice despite a marked increase in the number of CD11c+ cells.
source: Although a marked increase in the number of CD11c+ cells was observed in the anterior commissure of SIRPαKO mice, no appreciable demyelination was evident after immunostaining for myelin basic protein (MBP) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows CD11c staining alongside MBP staining, with no visible loss of MBP signal despite increased CD11c+ cells.

claim: Myelination in the corpus callosum and fimbria were normal in SIRPα KO mice when examined by myelin staining with Black-Gold II.
source: Myelination in the corpus callosum and fimbria were also normal in SIRPαKO mice when examined by myelin staining with a gold-phosphate complex (Black-Gold II) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Figure 2D shows Black-Gold staining of myelin in corpus callosum and fimbria, with no visible differences between WT and SIRPα KO mice.

claim: The yield of microglia from SIRPα KO mice was significantly greater than that from control mice.
source: The yield of microglia from SIRPα KO mice was significantly greater than that from control mice (means ± SEM were 8.02 ± 0.36 and 4.57 ± 0.98 × 104 cells/mouse, respectively; n = 5 for control and 3 for KO animals; p=0.02161 (Welch's t-test)), indicating an increased number of microglia in the spinal cord of SIRPα KO mice.
evidence: Statistical analysis of microglia yield shows significant difference (p=0.02161) between genotypes.

claim: CD11c+/CD11b+/CD45dim/lo microglia were increased in SIRPα KO mice when compared with control WT mice.
source: Consistent with the results from immunohistochemical analysis, CD11c+/CD11b+/CD45dim/lo microglia were increased in SIRPα KO mice when compared with control WT mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows flow cytometry data with quantification demonstrating statistically significant increase in CD11c+ microglia in SIRPα KO mice.

claim: The forward and side scatter distribution of CD11c+ microglia were similar to those of the CD11c– microglia in the SIRPα KO mice.
source: The forward (FSC) and side (SSC) scatter distribution of CD11c+ microglia were similar to those of the CD11c– microglia in the SIRPα KO mice, suggesting that cell size and granularity (complexity) were comparable between the two subsets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows FSC/SSC plots demonstrating similar distributions for CD11c+ and CD11c- microglia.

claim: CD11c+ microglia expressed higher levels of innate immune molecules (including CD14, Dectin-1, and CD68) when compared with CD11c− microglia in SIRPα KO mice.
source: CD11c+ microglia expressed higher levels of innate immune molecules (including CD14, Dectin-1, and CD68) when compared with CD11c− microglia in SIRPα KO mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows flow cytometry histograms demonstrating higher expression of CD14, Dectin-1, and CD68 in CD11c+ versus CD11c- microglia.

claim: The expression levels of SIRPα in microglia were comparable in aged and adult mice.
source: The expression levels of SIRPα in microglia were comparable in aged and adult mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3D shows flow cytometry histograms of SIRPα expression in adult versus aged mice with overlapping distributions.

claim: CD11c+ microglia were increased in aged mice when compared with adult mice.
source: CD11c+ microglia were increased in aged mice (as in SIRPα KO mice) when compared with adult mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: Figure 3E shows flow cytometry data with quantification demonstrating statistically significant increase in CD11c+ microglia in aged versus adult mice.

claim: The CD11c+ microglia in aged mice expressed higher levels of CD14, Dectin-1, and CD68 than the CD11c− microglia of these mice.
source: In addition, the CD11c+ microglia in the aged mice expressed higher levels of CD14, Dectin-1, and CD68 than the CD11c− microglia of these mice, as was also the case in SIRPα KO mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: Figure 3F shows flow cytometry histograms demonstrating higher expression of CD14, Dectin-1, and CD68 in CD11c+ versus CD11c- microglia from aged mice.

claim: The expression of TNF-α (Tnfa) was increased in SIRPα KO as compared to WT mice.
source: Among the examined cytokines (Tnfa, Il1b, Il6, Il10, and Tgfb), the expression of TNF-α (Tnfa) was increased in SIRPα KO as compared to WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows qPCR data demonstrating statistically significant increase in Tnfa expression in SIRPα KO mice.

claim: CD11c+ microglia were increased in the white matter of CD47 KO mice.
source: In the brain of CD47 KO mice, CD11c+ microglia were increased in the white matter, as was also the case for SIRPα KO mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows immunostaining demonstrating increased CD11c+ microglia in white matter of CD47 KO mice.

claim: The number of Iba1+ microglia was increased more than 2.5-fold in the hippocampal fimbria of CD47 KO mice.
source: The number of Iba1+ microglia was increased more than 2.5-fold in the hippocampal fimbria, and about 70% of the Iba1+ microglia expressed CD11c (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows quantification of Iba1+ and Iba1+/CD11c+ cells demonstrating statistically significant increases in CD47 KO mice.

claim: About 70% of the Iba1+ microglia expressed CD11c in the hippocampal fimbria of CD47 KO mice.
source: The number of Iba1+ microglia was increased more than 2.5-fold in the hippocampal fimbria, and about 70% of the Iba1+ microglia expressed CD11c (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows quantification data indicating approximately 70% of Iba1+ cells are also CD11c+ in CD47 KO mice.

claim: The yield of microglia in CD47 KO mice was increased compared to that in WT mice.
source: As in SIRPα KO mice, the yield of microglia in CD47 KO mice was increased compared to that in WT mice (means ± SEM were 7.65 ± 0.92 and 3.34 ± 0.85 × 104 cells/head, respectively; n = 5 animals; p=0.00874 (Welch's t-test)).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant difference (p=0.00874) in microglia yield between CD47 KO and WT mice.

claim: CD47 was expressed in WT microglia and was completely absent in CD47 KO microglia.
source: Flow cytometric analysis showed that CD47 was expressed in WT microglia and was completely absent in CD47 KO microglia (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows flow cytometry histograms demonstrating CD47 expression in WT but not in CD47 KO microglia.

claim: The expression of SIRPα was markedly increased in CD47 KO microglia.
source: In addition, we found that the expression of SIRPα was markedly increased in CD47 KO microglia (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows flow cytometry histograms demonstrating increased SIRPα expression in CD47 KO versus WT microglia.

claim: The expression of CD47 was increased in microglia prepared from SIRPα KO mice.
source: We also examined the expression of CD47 in SIRPα KO microglia, and found that the expression of CD47 was increased in microglia prepared from SIRPα KO mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4D shows flow cytometry histograms demonstrating increased CD47 expression in SIRPα KO versus WT microglia.

claim: The expression of 594 and 548 genes was markedly (>2 fold) increased and decreased, respectively, in CD47 KO mice white matter when compared with WT mice.
source: The expression of 594 and 548 genes was markedly (>2 fold) increased and decreased, respectively, in CD47 KO mice when compared with WT mice (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Microarray data analysis identified differentially expressed genes in white matter of CD47 KO mice.

claim: Genes whose expression increased in the white matter of CD47 KO mice were significantly enriched in pathways such as infectious diseases, phagocytosis, and immune responses.
source: Pathway analysis with Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) ver. 6.8 (https://david.ncifcrf.gov/) (Huang et al., 2009a; Huang et al., 2009b) suggested that the genes whose expression increased in the white matter of CD47 KO mice were significantly enriched in pathways such as infectious diseases, phagocytosis, and immune responses, probably reflecting the activation of microglia (Figure 5A).
evidence: Figure 5A shows KEGG pathway analysis results demonstrating enrichment of upregulated genes in immune-related pathways.

claim: Genes whose expression was decreased in CD47 KO mice white matter were mostly enriched in pathways for neuronal ligand–receptor interaction, calcium signaling and neuronal synapses.
source: By contrast, genes whose expression was decreased in CD47 KO mice were mostly enriched in pathways for neuronal ligand–receptor interaction, and were also enriched in pathways such as calcium signaling and neuronal synapses (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows KEGG pathway analysis results for downregulated genes in white matter.

claim: The expression of Itgax (CD11c), Clec7a (Dectin-1), Cd68, and Cd14 were markedly increased (>2-fold) in the white matter of CD47 KO mice compared with that of WT mice.
source: Consistent with the results of immunohistochemical and flow cytometric analyses, the expression of Itgax (CD11c), Clec7a (Dectin-1), Cd68, and Cd14 were markedly increased (>2-fold: Log2 ratio >1) in the white matter of CD47 KO mice compared with that of WT mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows Log2 ratio data from microarray analysis demonstrating >2-fold increases in these genes.

claim: The expression of the microglial markers Aif1 (Iba1) and Itgam (CD11b) was only moderately increased (<2 fold) in CD47 KO white matter.
source: By contrast, the expression of the microglial markers Aif1 (Iba1) and Itgam (CD11b) was only moderately increased (<2 fold).
evidence: Figure 5C shows Log2 ratio data indicating <1 (i.e., <2-fold) increase for Aif1 and Itgam.

claim: Several transcripts whose expression was reported to be increased in microglia during the repair of damaged myelin were markedly increased (>2 fold) in the white matter of CD47 KO mice.
source: We noted that several transcripts whose expression was reported to be increased in microglia during the repair of damaged myelin (Holtman et al., 2015; Olah et al., 2012; Poliani et al., 2015; Selvaraju et al., 2004) were markedly increased (>2 fold) in the white matter of CD47 KO mice (Figure 5C). These included Itgax, Lgals3, and Clec7a, markers of primed microglia; Lpl, Apoc1, and Ch25h, encoding molecules for lipid transport; Mmp12, encoding a tissue remodeling factor; Igf1, and Spp1, encoding trophic factors promoting oligodendrocyte differentiation; and Cst7 (Cystatin F), which encodes a cysteine proteinase inhibitor.
evidence: Figure 5C shows microarray data for these genes, and the claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Holtman et al., 2015; Olah et al., 2012; Poliani et al., 2015; Selvaraju et al., 2004).

claim: Several positive regulators of microglia phagocytosis, Trem2, Tyrobp, and Cx3cr1, were increased in the white matter of CD47 KO mice.
source: We also found that several positive regulators of microglia phagocytosis, Trem2, Tyrobp, and Cx3cr1 (Lampron et al., 2015; Poliani et al., 2015), were increased in the white matter of the mutant mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data (Figure 5C) and citations to prior literature (Lampron et al., 2015; Poliani et al., 2015) establishing these genes as phagocytosis regulators.

claim: Expression of a total 16,544 genes was detected in either CD47 KO and WT control brain mononuclear cells or both.
source: Expression of a total 16,544 genes was detected in either CD47 KO and WT control cells or both.
evidence: This is stated in the context of describing microarray analysis results for brain mononuclear cells.

claim: The expression of 1323 and 2286 genes was markedly (>2 fold) increased and decreased, respectively, in the CD47 KO brain mononuclear cells.
source: Among them, the expression of 1323 and 2286 genes was markedly (>2 fold) increased and decreased, respectively, in the CD47 KO cells (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Microarray data analysis identified differentially expressed genes in brain mononuclear cells of CD47 KO mice.

claim: Genes whose expression increased in CD47 KO brain cells were significantly enriched in pathways for T cell receptor signaling, axon guidance, proteoglycans in cancer, TNF signaling, and NF-κB signaling.
source: Genes whose expression increased in CD47 KO brain cells were significantly enriched in pathways for T cell receptor signaling, axon guidance, proteoglycans in cancer, TNF signaling, and NF-κB signaling (Figure 5A)
evidence: Figure 5A shows KEGG pathway analysis results for brain mononuclear cells.

claim: Genes whose expression decreased in CD47 KO brain cells were enriched in cancer-associated pathways including Wnt, Hippo, and Rap1 signaling, as well as cardiomyopathy.
source: genes whose expression decreased in CD47 KO brain cells were enriched in cancer-associated pathways including Wnt, Hippo, and Rap1 signaling, as well as cardiomyopathy (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows KEGG pathway analysis results for downregulated genes in brain mononuclear cells.

claim: 32 and 55 genes were commonly increased and decreased (>2 fold), respectively, in both the white matter and the brain mononuclear cells of CD47 KO mice.
source: Comparison of array data revealed 32 and 55 genes that were commonly increased and decreased (>2 fold), respectively, in both the white matter and the brain mononuclear cells of CD47 KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2 lists the commonly changed genes between the two tissue types.

claim: Shared induced genes between white matter and brain mononuclear cells included myelin-repair related genes, such as Itgax, Igf1, Lpl, Apoc1, Ch25h, Mmp12, Spp1, and Cst7.
source: Shared induced genes included myelin-repair related genes, such as Itgax, Igf1, Lpl, Apoc1, Ch25h, Mmp12, Spp1, and Cst7 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows expression data for these genes in both white matter and brain mononuclear cells.

claim: Quantitative PCR analysis of selected genes (Itgax, Igf1, Trem2, Ccl3) showed significant induction in CD47 KO white matter.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis of selected genes (Itgax, Igf1, Trem2, Ccl3), which were increased in the microarray analysis, also showed significant induction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows qPCR validation data demonstrating statistically significant increases in these genes.

claim: More than 98% of microglia were SIRPα-negative in the brain of tamoxifen-treated SIRPα-flox:Cx3cr1–CreERT2 mice.
source: Flow-cytometric analysis revealed that more than 98% of microglia were SIRPα-negative in the brain of tamoxifen-treated SIRPα-flox:Cx3cr1–CreERT2 mice (Figure 6A)
evidence: Figure 6A shows flow cytometry data demonstrating 1.69% SIRPα+ microglia in SIRPα cKO mice versus 90.9% in control.

claim: The numbers of Iba1+, Iba1+/CD11c+, and Iba1+/CD68+ microglia were increased in the hippocampal fimbria of SIRPα cKO mice.
source: Flow-cytometric analysis revealed that more than 98% of microglia were SIRPα-negative in the brain of tamoxifen-treated SIRPα-flox:Cx3cr1–CreERT2 mice (Figure 6A), and that the numbers of Iba1+, Iba1+/CD11c+, and Iba1+/CD68+ microglia were increased in the hippocampal fimbria of these cKO mice (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Figure 6B and C show immunostaining and quantification demonstrating statistically significant increases in these cell populations.

claim: Iba1+/CD11c+ cells were detected in white-matter regions of the brain and spinal cord in SIRPα cKO, but not in control SIRPα-flox:— mice.
source: Iba1+/CD11c+ cells were also detected in other white-matter regions of the brain and spinal cord in SIRPα cKO, but not in control SIRPα-flox:— mice, and were barely detected in the grey matter of both genotypes (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Figure 6D and E show immunostaining of brain and spinal cord sections demonstrating CD11c+ cells in white matter of cKO but not control mice.

claim: Iba1+/CD11c+ cells were barely detected in the grey matter of both SIRPα cKO and control genotypes.
source: Iba1+/CD11c+ cells were also detected in other white-matter regions of the brain and spinal cord in SIRPα cKO, but not in control SIRPα-flox:— mice, and were barely detected in the grey matter of both genotypes (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Figure 6D shows minimal CD11c signal in grey matter (ctx) of both genotypes.

claim: CD11c+ microglia in SIRPα cKO mice expressed higher levels of CD14, Dectin-1, and CD68 when compared with CD11c− microglia.
source: Flow cytometric analysis in SIRPα cKO mice showed that, when compared with CD11c− microglia, CD11c+ microglia expressed higher levels of CD14, Dectin-1, and CD68 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1 shows flow cytometry histograms demonstrating higher expression of these markers in CD11c+ versus CD11c- microglia.

claim: A lack of the interaction between SIRPα on microglia and CD47 on neighbouring cells is the primary cause of the induction of CD11c+ microglia in CD47–SIRPα signal-deficient mice.
source: All of these results were very similar to those observed in SIRPα null KO mice, and suggest that a lack of the interaction between SIRPα on microglia and CD47 on neighbouring cells is the primary cause of the induction of CD11c+ microglia in CD47–SIRPα signal-deficient mice.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the similarity of phenotypes between SIRPα null KO, CD47 KO, and microglia-specific SIRPα cKO mice, all showing increased CD11c+ microglia.

claim: The emergence of CD11c+ microglia was not observed in the CD11c+ cell-specific SIRPα cKO mice.
source: However, the emergence of CD11c+ microglia was not observed in the CD11c+ cell-specific SIRPα cKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the expansion of resident CD11c+ microglia was not induced by the lack of SIRPα.
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 2 shows immunostaining of CD11c+ cell-specific SIRPα cKO mice with no increase in CD11c+ cells.

claim: The ablation of SIRPα in CD11c-negative microglia induced the expression of CD11c in these cells.
source: It is likely that the ablation of SIRPα in CD11c-negative microglia induced the expression of CD11c in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CD11c+ cell-specific SIRPα cKO did not show increased CD11c+ microglia, while microglia-specific cKO did.

claim: The frequency of myelinated axons in the anterior commissure was comparable between SIRPα cKO and control mice.
source: In the cross-section of the anterior commissure (Figure 7A), the frequency of myelinated axons and the g-ratio (the ratio of the inneraxonal diameter to the total outer diameter) (Figure 7B) were comparable between SIRPα cKO and control mice (frequency of myelinated axons 34.6 ± 4.37% for control (n = 3), 36.6 ± 4.05% for cKO (n = 3), p=0.759, Welch's t-test
evidence: Figure 7A and B show electron microscopy images and quantification with no significant difference (p=0.759) between genotypes.

claim: The g-ratio was comparable between SIRPα cKO and control mice in the anterior commissure.
source: In the cross-section of the anterior commissure (Figure 7A), the frequency of myelinated axons and the g-ratio (the ratio of the inneraxonal diameter to the total outer diameter) (Figure 7B) were comparable between SIRPα cKO and control mice (frequency of myelinated axons 34.6 ± 4.37% for control (n = 3), 36.6 ± 4.05% for cKO (n = 3), p=0.759, Welch's t-test; g-ratio 0.63 ± 0.026 for control (n = 3), 0.65 ± 0.009 for cKO (n = 3), p=0.448, Welch's t-test).
evidence: Figure 7B shows quantification with no significant difference (p=0.448) in g-ratio between genotypes.

claim: A scatter plot of all g-ratio data as a function of axon diameters was comparable between SIRPα cKO and control genotypes.
source: A scatter plot of all g-ratio data as a function of axon diameters was also comparable between the two genotypes (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7C shows overlapping scatter plots for control and cKO mice.

claim: The myelin structure was normal in the SIRPα cKO mice.
source: These data suggest that the myelin structure was normal in the mutant mice.
evidence: This conclusion is based on electron microscopy analysis showing comparable myelination frequency and g-ratios (Figure 7A-C).

claim: Feeding with cuprizone for 5 weeks induced demyelination accompanied by the robust accumulation of microglia in white matter regions in control mice.
source: Feeding with Cpz, a copper chelator, for 5 weeks induced demyelination accompanied by the robust accumulation of microglia (microgliosis) in white matter regions (including the hippocampal alveus and corpus callosum) in control mice as previously reported (Figure 8A) (Gudi et al., 2014; Norkute et al., 2009).
evidence: Figure 8A shows immunostaining demonstrating demyelination and microgliosis after 5 weeks of cuprizone treatment. The claim is also supported by citations to prior literature (Gudi et al., 2014; Norkute et al., 2009).

claim: CD11c+/Iba1+ microglia were markedly increased in number at the site of microgliosis in control mice after cuprizone treatment.
source: At the site of microgliosis, CD11c+/Iba1+ microglia were markedly increased in number, even in control mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: Figure 8A shows immunostaining demonstrating increased CD11c signal in white matter regions after cuprizone treatment.

claim: Both demyelination and microgliosis were significantly reduced in SIRPα cKO mice after 5 weeks of cuprizone treatment.
source: In SIRPα cKO mice, both demyelination and microgliosis were significantly reduced after the same treatment (Figure 8A-C).
evidence: Figure 8A-C show immunostaining and quantification demonstrating statistically significant reductions in demyelination and microgliosis in SIRPα cKO versus control mice.

claim: SIRPα cKO mice showed a tendency to reduce the size of the CD11c-positive area compared to that in control mice after 5 weeks of cuprizone treatment, although this change was not statistically significant.
source: At this time point, SIRPα cKO mice also showed a tendency to reduce the size of the CD11c-positive area compared to that in control mice, although this change was not statistically significant (Figure 8D).
evidence: Figure 8D shows quantification of CD11c+ area at 5 weeks with no statistically significant difference between genotypes.

claim: Demyelination was not observed in control or SIRPα cKO mice after 3 weeks of cuprizone treatment.
source: At an early stage of Cpz treatment (after 3 wks feeding with Cpz), demyelination was not observed in control or SIRPα cKO mice (Figure 8A)
evidence: Figure 8A shows MBP staining at 3 weeks with no visible demyelination in either genotype.

claim: Abnormally strong immunoreactivity of MBP was observed in both control and SIRPα cKO mice after 3 weeks of cuprizone treatment.
source: At an early stage of Cpz treatment (after 3 wks feeding with Cpz), demyelination was not observed in control or SIRPα cKO mice (Figure 8A), but abnormally strong immunoreactivity of MBP was observed in these mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: Figure 8A shows asterisks indicating abnormally strong MBP immunoreactivity at 3 weeks in both genotypes.

claim: The abnormally strong immunoreactivity of MBP after 3 weeks of cuprizone treatment was probably related to myelin damage.
source: This was probably related to myelin damage, because the epitope of the anti-MBP antibody that we used (DENPVV) is similar to that of a myelin damage-detectable antibody (QDENPVV) (Matsuo et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Matsuo et al., 1998) describing antibody epitopes.

claim: Significant microgliosis and an increase in CD11c-positive area size were observed in both genotypes after 3 weeks of cuprizone treatment.
source: Consistently, significant microgliosis, as well as an increase in CD11c-positive area size, was observed in both genotypes after 3 wks feeding with Cpz (Figures 8A, C and D).
evidence: Figures 8A, C and D show immunostaining and quantification demonstrating increased Iba1+ and CD11c+ areas at 3 weeks.

claim: Both microgliosis and CD11c-positive area sizes were comparable between SIRPα cKO and control mice after 3 weeks of cuprizone treatment.
source: At this stage, both of these parameters (sizes of Iba1-positive area (microgliosis) and CD11c-positive area) were comparable between the two genotypes (Figures 8A, C and D).
evidence: Figures 8C and D show quantification at 3 weeks with no statistically significant differences between genotypes.

claim: The repair of demyelination was observed after feeding with normal chow for 2 weeks following 5 weeks of cuprizone treatment.
source: The repair of demyelination was observed after feeding with normal chow for 2 wks (Figure 8A).
evidence: Figure 8A shows MBP staining at recovery time point (Rec 2 wks) with restoration of myelin signal.

claim: Iba1-positive and CD11c-positive area sizes in white matter were still larger than those in the basal condition at 2 weeks recovery in both genotypes.
source: At this time point, Iba1-positive (microgliosis) and CD11c-positive area sizes in white matter were still larger than those in the basal condition (without feeding of Cpz) in both genotypes (Figures 8A, C and D).
evidence: Figures 8C and D show quantification at recovery time point with elevated values compared to basal condition.

claim: No statistical difference between SIRPα cKO mice and control mice was found for Iba1+ and CD11c+ area sizes at 2 weeks recovery.
source: No statistical difference between SIRPα cKO mice and control mice was found for these parameters, whereas the size of the Iba1+ area showed the tendency to be reduced in SIRPα cKO when compared to that in control mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: Figures 8C and D show quantification at recovery time point with no statistically significant differences, though a trend is noted for Iba1+ area.

claim: The number of Olig2+ cells in white matter was significantly decreased after 3 weeks of cuprizone feeding.
source: In the white matter, the number of cells expressing Olig2+, a pan-oligodendrocyte marker(Nishiyama et al., 2009), was significantly decreased after 3 wks of Cpz feeding, suggesting that demyelination was preceded by the loss of oligodendrocytes (Figure 8A and E).
evidence: Figure 8E shows quantification demonstrating statistically significant decrease in Olig2+ cells at 3 weeks in both genotypes. The claim is also supported by citation to prior literature (Nishiyama et al., 2009) establishing Olig2 as an oligodendrocyte marker.

claim: The number of Olig2+ cells was increased after 5 weeks of cuprizone treatment and recovered to normal levels after another two weeks of feeding with normal chow.
source: The number of Olig2+ cells was increased after 5 wks of Cpz treatment and recovered to normal levels after another two weeks of feeding with normal chow.
evidence: Figure 8E shows quantification of Olig2+ cells across time points demonstrating recovery.

claim: No significant differences in the number of Olig2+ cells were noted between control and SIRPα cKO mice throughout the de- and re-myelination process.
source: Throughout the de- and re-myelination process, no significant differences in the number of Olig2+ cells were noted between control and SIRPα cKO mice.
evidence: Figure 8E shows quantification with no statistically significant differences between genotypes at any time point.

claim: SIRPα is a key molecule for the suppression of microglia activation in vivo.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that SIRPα is a key molecule for the suppression of microglia activation in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that genetic ablation of SIRPα (null KO and microglia-specific cKO) results in increased microglia activation and CD11c+ microglia emergence.

claim: SIRPα proteins that are expressed on microglia directly control microglia activation and the induction of CD11c+ microglia in vivo.
source: Microglia-specific SIRPα cKO mice exhibited the same phenotype as SIRPα null KO mice. Therefore, SIRPα proteins that are expressed on microglia directly control microglia activation and the induction of CD11c+ microglia in vivo.
evidence: The similarity of phenotypes between null KO and microglia-specific cKO mice demonstrates that microglial SIRPα is responsible for the observed effects.

claim: CD11c+ microglia are derived from resident microglia in the brain, and are not recruited monocytes.
source: The emergence of CD11c+ microglia in the brains of microglia-specific SIRPα cKO mice establishes that CD11c+ microglia are derived from resident microglia in the brain, and are not recruited monocytes that are spared in the TAM-induced system (Goldmann et al., 2013; Safaiyan et al., 2016; Wolf et al., 2013).
evidence: The use of the Cx3cr1-CreERT2 system with tamoxifen treatment specifically targets resident microglia while sparing peripheral monocytes, as established by cited literature (Goldmann et al., 2013; Safaiyan et al., 2016; Wolf et al., 2013).

claim: The characteristics of CD11c+ microglia in SIRPα mutant mice were similar to those of the 'primed microglia' that have been observed in aging and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: The characteristics of CD11c+ microglia in our mutant mice were similar to those of the 'primed microglia' that have been observed in aging and neurodegenerative diseases (Holtman et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of gene expression and marker profiles with those described in cited literature (Holtman et al., 2015).

claim: SIRPα is a possible key component of the regulation of microglia priming in vivo.
source: The characteristics of CD11c+ microglia in our mutant mice were similar to those of the 'primed microglia' that have been observed in aging and neurodegenerative diseases (Holtman et al., 2015); thus, SIRPα is a possible key component of the regulation of microglia priming in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of CD11c+ microglia in SIRPα mutants to primed microglia described in literature.

claim: The CD47–SIRPα interaction is important for the suppression of microglia activation in the brain.
source: However, we found that CD47 KO mice exhibited a phenotype similar to that of SIRPα KO mice, suggesting that the CD47–SIRPα interaction is indeed important for the suppression of microglia activation in the brain.
evidence: The similarity of phenotypes between CD47 KO and SIRPα KO mice demonstrates the importance of this specific ligand-receptor interaction.

claim: The CD47 signal may have a SIRPα-independent function that suppresses the proliferation of microglia.
source: Interestingly, the number of Iba1-positive cells in the fimbria of CD47 KO mice was greater than that in SIRPα null KO or cKO mice, whereas the number of CD11c/Iba1 double-positive cells was comparable in CD47 KO and SIRPα cKO mice (Figure 1B, Figure 4B, and Figure 6C). The CD47 signal may have a SIRPα-independent function that suppresses the proliferation of microglia.
evidence: The differential effect on total Iba1+ cells versus CD11c+/Iba1+ cells between CD47 KO and SIRPα KO mice suggests an additional function of CD47.

claim: Lack of interaction between CD47 and SIRPα may result in the upregulated expression of SIRPα or CD47 in microglia as a compensatory response.
source: Lack of interaction between CD47 and SIRPα may result in the upregulated expression of SIRPα or CD47 in microglia as a compensatory response, or in the stabilization of the CD47–SIRPα complex on microglia, because our previous study suggested that the interaction between CD47 and SIRPα induced endocytosis of the CD47–SIRPα complex in CHO cells (Kusakari et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculated based on observed increased expression of SIRPα in CD47 KO microglia and CD47 in SIRPα KO microglia, and supported by citation to prior work (Kusakari et al., 2008) on CD47-SIRPα complex endocytosis.

claim: CD11c+ microglia are increased during postnatal development and normal aging.
source: The appearance of CD11c+ microglia has also been reported during postnatal development and normal aging (Bulloch et al., 2008; Kaunzner et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Bulloch et al., 2008; Kaunzner et al., 2012).

claim: CD11c+ microglia characteristically appeared in the brain white matter during postnatal development and aging.
source: In both cases, CD11c+ microglia characteristically appeared in the brain white matter, where myelin construction during the late developmental stage (Baumann and Pham-Dinh, 2001) or the accumulation of damaged myelin debris during aging were remarkable (Safaiyan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Baumann and Pham-Dinh, 2001; Safaiyan et al., 2016).

claim: Demyelination markedly induced CD11c+ microglia in the adult brain.
source: It was also shown that demyelination markedly induced CD11c+ microglia, even in the adult brain (Remington et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Remington et al., 2007).

claim: The induction of CD11c+ microglia during demyelination was suppressed in mutant mice lacking Trem2 or Cx3Cr1.
source: It was also shown that demyelination markedly induced CD11c+ microglia, even in the adult brain (Remington et al., 2007), but this induction was suppressed in mutant mice lacking Trem2 or Cx3Cr1 (Lampron et al., 2015; Poliani et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Lampron et al., 2015; Poliani et al., 2015).

claim: The clearance of myelin debris was markedly impaired in Trem2 and Cx3Cr1 mutant mice.
source: Of note, the clearance of myelin debris was markedly impaired in these mutant mice (Cantoni et al., 2015; Lampron et al., 2015; Poliani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cantoni et al., 2015; Lampron et al., 2015; Poliani et al., 2015).

claim: CD11c+ microglia accumulate around amyloid plaques in an AD mouse model.
source: CD11c+ microglia also accumulate around amyloid plaques in an AD mouse model that has gene expression patterns indicating an enhanced capacity for phagocytosis (Kamphuis et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Kamphuis et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: The phagocytic ability of CD11c+ microglia might contribute to the removal and repair of damaged tissues.
source: The phagocytic ability of CD11c+ microglia thus might contribute to the removal and repair of damaged tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from observations that CD11c+ microglia have enhanced phagocytic markers and appear in contexts of tissue damage and repair.

claim: SIRPα is a membrane protein that is highly expressed in macrophages and dendritic cells.
source: SIRPα (CD172a) is a membrane protein that is highly expressed in macrophages and dendritic cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SIRPα expression patterns.

claim: The extracellular region of SIRPα specifically interacts with CD47 to promote cell–cell contact signals.
source: The extracellular region of SIRPα specifically interacts with another membrane protein CD47 to promote cell–cell contact signals (Matozaki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Matozaki et al., 2009).

claim: Interactions between SIRPα on phagocytic cells and CD47 on phagocytosed targets act as a 'don't eat me' signal.
source: Interactions between SIRPα on phagocytic cells and CD47 on phagocytosed targets, such as erythrocytes, cancer cells, and apoptotic cells, act as a 'don't eat me' signal and thereby control erythrocyte homeostasis, elimination of cancer cells, and the formation of arteriosclerotic plaques (Chao et al., 2011; Ishikawa-Sekigami et al., 2006; Kojima et al., 2016; Willingham et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Chao et al., 2011; Ishikawa-Sekigami et al., 2006; Kojima et al., 2016; Willingham et al., 2012).

claim: SIRPα and CD47 are abundantly expressed on neurons in the brain.
source: In the brain, SIRPα and CD47 are abundantly expressed on neurons (Ohnishi et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Ohnishi et al., 2010).

claim: SIRPα is expressed on microglia.
source: In the brain, SIRPα and CD47 are abundantly expressed on neurons (Ohnishi et al., 2010), and SIRPα is also expressed on microglia (Gitik et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Gitik et al., 2011).

claim: SIRPα on microglia interacts with neuronal CD47 to suppress microglial activation.
source: It is assumed that SIRPα on microglia interacts with neuronal CD47 to suppress microglial activation (Saijo and Glass, 2011), because SIRPα contains an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif (ITIM) in its cytoplasmic region (Barclay and Hatherley, 2008; Matozaki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Saijo and Glass, 2011; Barclay and Hatherley, 2008; Matozaki et al., 2009).

claim: SIRPα on microglia controls cell activation through the interaction with its ligand CD47 and negatively regulates the induction of CD11c+ microglia in white but not in grey matter.
source: Specifically, our results establish that SIRPα on microglia controls cell activation through the interaction with its ligand CD47 and negatively regulates the induction of CD11c+ microglia, which have the potential to support the repair of damaged myelin, in white but not in grey matter.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental findings showing white matter-specific emergence of CD11c+ microglia in SIRPα and CD47 deficient mice.

claim: CD11c+ microglia have the potential to support the repair of damaged myelin.
source: Specifically, our results establish that SIRPα on microglia controls cell activation through the interaction with its ligand CD47 and negatively regulates the induction of CD11c+ microglia, which have the potential to support the repair of damaged myelin, in white but not in grey matter.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data showing upregulation of myelin repair-associated genes in CD47 KO mice and by the alleviation of cuprizone-induced demyelination in SIRPα cKO mice.

claim: Cuprizone-induced demyelination was alleviated by the microglia-specific ablation of SIRPα.
source: In addition, cuprizone-induced demyelination was alleviated by the microglia-specific ablation of SIRPα.
evidence: Figure 8A-C show reduced demyelination in SIRPα cKO mice after cuprizone treatment.

claim: Microglial SIRPα suppresses the induction of CD11c+ microglia that have the potential to accelerate the repair of damaged white matter.
source: Thus, microglial SIRPα suppresses the induction of CD11c+ microglia that have the potential to accelerate the repair of damaged white matter.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that loss of SIRPα leads to increased CD11c+ microglia and reduced demyelination damage in the cuprizone model.
